questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed three times and $X$ denotes the number of tails. Then $P(X=2)$ is
questions.explanation: A fair coin tossed three times has $2^3=8$ equally likely outcomes, since each toss has two results. Exactly two tails means choosing which two of the three tosses show tails, which can be done in $\binom32=3$ ways: HTT, THT and TTH. Dividing favourable outcomes by total outcomes gives $P(X=2)=\dfrac38$.

optionRationale.1: This counts only two of the three favourable outcomes, giving $2/8$.
optionRationale.2: This is the probability of one specific number of tails being possible, $4/8$, not of exactly two.
optionRationale.4: This is the probability of a single outcome such as TTH, not of the whole event.

questions.stem: A random variable $X$ takes the values $1,2,3$ with probabilities $0.5,\ 0.3,\ 0.2$ respectively. The mean of $X$ is
questions.explanation: The mean is $\sum xp=1(0.5)+2(0.3)+3(0.2)=0.5+0.6+0.6=1.7$. The mean is pulled towards the value $1$ because that value has the largest probability.

optionRationale.1: This is the simple average of $1,2,3$, ignoring the unequal probabilities.
optionRationale.4: This is the sum of the probabilities, not the mean.

questions.stem: Machine A makes 60% of the items in a factory and Machine B makes 40%. Of the items from A, 2% are defective, and of the items from B, 5% are defective. An item chosen at random is found defective. The probability that it came from Machine B is
questions.explanation: Machine A supplies $0.6\times0.02=0.012$ defective items for every unit of output, and Machine B supplies $0.4\times0.05=0.020$. A defective item must be one of these, so by Bayes' theorem the chance that it came from B is B's share of the total: $\dfrac{0.020}{0.012+0.020}=\dfrac{0.020}{0.032}=\dfrac58$. B's higher defect rate outweighs its smaller share of output.

optionRationale.1: This is $P(A\mid D)=\dfrac{0.012}{0.032}$, the probability that the item came from Machine A.
optionRationale.2: This is the prior probability $0.4$ of B, which ignores that B has the higher defect rate.
optionRationale.3: This assumes both machines are equally likely to be the source, ignoring the data.

questions.explanation: For $B(8,\tfrac12)$ the mean is $np=4$ (II) and the variance is $npq=8\cdot\tfrac14=2$ (III). For $B(3,\tfrac12)$, $P(X=0)=\left(\tfrac12\right)^3=\tfrac18$ (IV). For $B(2,\tfrac12)$, $P(X=1)=2\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac12$ (I).

optionRationale.1: This swaps the mean and the variance of the distribution; the mean is $np$ and the variance is $npq$.
optionRationale.3: This swaps the last two values; $P(X=0)$ for $n=3$ is $\tfrac18$, not $\tfrac12$.
optionRationale.4: This gives the variance the value $\tfrac12$, which is smaller than $npq=2$ for $n=8$.

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): If $X$ follows $B\!\left(5,\tfrac12\right)$, then $P(X=2)=P(X=3)$.
Reason (R): The sum of the probabilities of all values of a random variable in a probability distribution is 1.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: For $B(5,\tfrac12)$, $P(X=2)=\binom52/32=\tfrac{10}{32}$ and $P(X=3)=\binom53/32=\tfrac{10}{32}$, so they are equal and the assertion is true (by symmetry, since $p=\tfrac12$). The reason is a true property of every distribution, but it does not explain the equality.

optionRationale.1: The sum rule does not explain the equality; the equality comes from $\binom52=\binom53$ when $p=\tfrac12$.
optionRationale.3: The reason is true, so this option is wrong.
optionRationale.4: The assertion is true, since both probabilities equal $\tfrac{10}{32}$.

questions.stem: A fair die is thrown 4 times. The probability of getting at least one six is
questions.explanation: The complement is 'no six in four throws', whose probability is $\left(\tfrac56\right)^4=\dfrac{625}{1296}$. So the required probability is $1-\dfrac{625}{1296}=\dfrac{671}{1296}$.

optionRationale.1: This is the probability of no six at all, the complement of the required event.
optionRationale.2: This is $4\cdot\tfrac16$, adding the probabilities of a six on each throw, which overcounts overlapping cases.
optionRationale.3: This is the probability of at least one six in just two throws, not four.

questions.stem: The mean and the variance of a binomial random variable are $12$ and $3$ respectively. The probability of success in a single trial is
questions.explanation: We have $np=12$ and $npq=3$. Dividing, $q=\dfrac{3}{12}=\dfrac14$, so $p=1-q=\dfrac34$. Then $n=12\div\tfrac34=16$, and indeed $npq=16\cdot\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac14=3$.

optionRationale.2: This is $q$, the probability of failure, found from the ratio but not subtracted from $1$.
optionRationale.3: This would make the variance equal to the mean divided by $2$, which does not give $3$ for a mean of $12$.
optionRationale.4: This is $\tfrac{npq}{n}$ with $n=16$, which is $pq$, not $p$.

questions.stem: In a population 1% of people have a certain disease. A test detects the disease in 90% of those who have it and wrongly gives a positive result for 5% of those who do not. A person tests positive. The probability that the person has the disease is
questions.explanation: Out of $10000$ people, $100$ have the disease and $90$ of them test positive. Of the $9900$ healthy people, $5\%$ (about $495$) also test positive. So only $90$ of the $585$ positives are really ill, giving $\dfrac{90}{585}=\dfrac2{13}$. Bayes' theorem gives the same value, $\dfrac{0.009}{0.009+0.0495}$. Because the disease is rare, false positives outnumber true ones.

optionRationale.1: This is $P(+\mid\text{disease})$, the sensitivity of the test, not the probability of disease given a positive result.
optionRationale.2: This uses $0.9\times0.05=0.045$ for the false positives, a slip that should be $0.99\times0.05$, giving $\dfrac{0.009}{0.054}$.
optionRationale.4: This uses $0.05$ for the false-positive contribution without multiplying by the $99\%$ who are healthy.
